scenes.label: Session 3 · Lean Startup
scenes.title: Lean Startup: the scientific method for building a business
scenes.subtitle: From hypotheses to product–market fit, and to a go-to-market strategy you have tested

beats.say: Welcome. In this video we look at Lean Startup from a particular angle: as the scientific method, adapted to building a business. We will see how it takes you to product–market fit, and how it shapes your go-to-market strategy.

scenes.label: 01 · Why science?
scenes.sub: Eric Ries defines a startup as an organisation creating something new under extreme uncertainty. When nobody knows the answer, you need a method for finding it.

beats.say: Eric Ries defines a startup as an organisation that creates a new product or service under conditions of extreme uncertainty.
When nobody knows the answer, opinions and plans are not enough. You need a method for finding the answer. Humanity already has one: the scientific method. Lean Startup adapts it to business.

scenes.label: The method
scenes.title: From the scientific method to Lean Startup
rows: Customer discovery: get out of the building

beats.say: Look at the two methods side by side. A scientist starts by observing. A founder does the same: customer discovery, which Steve Blank summarises as get out of the building.
A scientist writes a hypothesis that can be proven wrong. A founder writes down the leap-of-faith assumptions the business depends on.
The scientist runs an experiment. The founder builds a minimum viable product: the smallest experiment that tests the hypothesis with real customers.
Then both analyse the results against the prediction. In Lean Startup this is called innovation accounting.
And both conclude. The scientist accepts or rejects the hypothesis. The founder perseveres or pivots.

scenes.label: Hypotheses
scenes.title: Two leap-of-faith assumptions

cards.title: Value hypothesis
cards.text: Does the product really deliver value to customers once they use it?

cards.title: Growth hypothesis
cards.text: How will new customers discover the product, and keep coming?

scenes.banner: Test the riskiest one first, and write it so that it can be proven wrong.

beats.say: Ries says every business plan rests on two leap-of-faith assumptions. The value hypothesis: does the product really deliver value once customers use it?
And the growth hypothesis: how will new customers discover it, and keep coming?
Test the riskiest one first. And write it the way a scientist would: so that it can be proven wrong.

scenes.label: Hypotheses
scenes.title: Write hypotheses that can fail
scenes.example: We believe that wind-farm maintenance managers will pay 20 € per turbine per month for failure alerts. We are right if 3 of 10 pilot farms sign a contract after a three-month trial.

beats.say: A useful hypothesis has four parts. A specific customer. A behaviour you can observe, not an opinion. One metric. And a threshold with a date, decided before you run the test.

For example: we believe that wind-farm maintenance managers will pay twenty euros per turbine per month for failure alerts. We are right if three of ten pilot farms sign a contract after a three-month trial. If they don't, the hypothesis is rejected, and you have learned something.

scenes.label: The experiment loop
scenes.title: Build – Measure – Learn, planned in reverse

nodes.title: Learn
nodes.text: First decide what you need to learn: which hypothesis?

nodes.title: Measure
nodes.text: Then decide which metric would prove it right or wrong.

nodes.title: Build
nodes.text: Only then build the smallest MVP that produces that metric.

beats.say: The experiment loop is build, measure, learn. But Ries points out that you should plan it in reverse. First, decide what you need to learn: which hypothesis are you testing?
Then decide what you need to measure to prove it right or wrong.
Only then decide what to build: the smallest product that can produce that measurement. Anything more is waste.

steps.title: Smoke test
steps.text: A landing page for a product that does not exist yet. Measures sign-ups.

steps.title: Concierge
steps.text: Deliver the service by hand to a few customers. Measures value.

steps.title: Wizard of Oz
steps.text: Looks automated, humans behind the curtain. Measures usage.

steps.title: Pre-order
steps.text: Ask for payment before building. Measures willingness to pay.

steps.title: A/B test
steps.text: Two versions, split traffic. Measures which one works better.

beats.say: An MVP is not a small version of your product. It is an experiment, and there are many kinds. A smoke test: a landing page for a product that does not exist yet.
A concierge MVP: you deliver the service by hand to a handful of customers.
A Wizard of Oz MVP: it looks automated, but humans do the work behind the curtain.
A pre-order: ask for money before you build. Nothing measures willingness to pay better.
And the A/B test: two versions, split traffic, and see which one performs better. This is the controlled experiment of the scientific method.

scenes.label: Innovation accounting
scenes.title: Measure like a scientist: actionable, not vanity, metrics
rows: Users still active after four weeks
Customers who paid, renewed or referred someone
scenes.banner: Good metrics are actionable, accessible and auditable: they show cause and effect, everyone understands them, and they can be checked.

beats.say: Analysing results is where many teams fool themselves. Vanity metrics, like total sign-ups or page views, always go up and make you feel good. They tell you nothing about cause and effect.
Actionable metrics do: weekly active users by cohort, the conversion rate of each experiment, how many users are still active after four weeks.
And replace opinions like customers love it with behaviour: who paid, who renewed, who referred someone.
Ries asks for metrics that are actionable, accessible and auditable: they show cause and effect, everyone understands them, and anyone can check them.

cards.title: Persevere
cards.text: The evidence supports the hypothesis: keep going and test the next riskiest one.

cards.title: Pivot
cards.text: Part of the model is wrong: change one element and keep what you learned.

cards.title: Stop
cards.text: The core hypothesis is rejected: stop, and spend the time on a better idea.

beats.say: Every experiment ends with a decision. Persevere: the evidence supports the hypothesis, so keep going, and test the next riskiest assumption.
Pivot: part of the model is wrong. Change one element, like the segment, the channel or the revenue model, and keep what you learned.
Or stop. A rejected hypothesis is not a failure of the method. It is the method working, and it frees your time for a better idea.

scenes.label: 02 · Product–market fit
scenes.text: “Being in a good market with a product that can satisfy that market.”
scenes.sub: Marc Andreessen, 2007. Lean Startup is the method for searching for that fit.

beats.say: So where does all this experimenting lead? To product–market fit. Marc Andreessen defined it in 2007 as being in a good market, with a product that can satisfy that market.
Product–market fit is the destination. Lean Startup is the method for getting there: each experiment brings you closer, or tells you to change direction.

scenes.label: Product–market fit
scenes.title: Three signals that you have product–market fit

cards.title: The Sean Ellis test
cards.text: At least 40% of users would be very disappointed if they could no longer use the product.

cards.title: Retention flattens
cards.text: Each cohort's usage curve stops falling and stays flat: people keep coming back.

cards.title: Market pull
cards.text: Customers find you by word of mouth, sales cycles get shorter, and you can't keep up with demand.

beats.say: How do you know you have it? Three signals. First, the Sean Ellis test: ask users how they would feel if they could no longer use the product. If at least forty percent say very disappointed, you are probably there.
Second, retention. Plot each cohort of users over time. When the curve stops falling and goes flat, people are coming back because they need the product.
Third, pull. Customers find you by word of mouth, sales get easier, and it feels like the market is pulling the product out of your hands.

scenes.label: Customer development
scenes.title: Search first, then execute

steps.title: Customer discovery
steps.text: Is there a problem worth solving, and for whom?

steps.title: Customer validation
steps.text: Will they use it and pay? Is the model repeatable?

steps.title: Customer creation
steps.text: Create demand and scale the go-to-market.

steps.title: Company building
steps.text: From a search team to a company that executes.

scenes.banner: Product–market fit is the line between searching and executing. Scaling before it burns money.

beats.say: Steve Blank's customer development model shows where fit sits. The first two steps are about searching. Customer discovery: is there a problem worth solving, and for whom?
Customer validation: will they use it, will they pay, and can you repeat the sale?
Only then do you execute. Customer creation: build demand and scale your go-to-market.
And company building: turn a team that searches into a company that executes.
Product–market fit is the line between searching and executing. Most startups that fail scale too early: they pour money into marketing and sales before the product fits.

scenes.label: 03 · Go-to-market
scenes.title: Your go-to-market strategy is a set of hypotheses too
rows: This segment needs it most, and buys first
Interviews and one landing page per segment
This value proposition makes them act
A/B test two messages in ads or e-mails
We can reach them here at an acceptable cost
Small budget per channel; measure cost per customer
Paid pilots with clear success criteria

beats.say: Here is where Lean Startup meets go-to-market strategy. A go-to-market plan answers five questions: who do we sell to first, with what message, through which channel, at what price, and how do we close the sale. Each answer is a hypothesis.
Which segment needs it most and will buy first? That is your beachhead. Test it with interviews and a separate landing page per segment.
Which message makes them act? A/B test two value propositions in ads or e-mails.
Which channel reaches them at an acceptable cost? Spend a small budget on each, and measure what it costs to get one customer.
What will they pay? Test with pre-orders or two price levels. And for business customers, does a pilot turn into a contract? Run paid pilots with clear success criteria.

scenes.label: Go-to-market
scenes.title: Choose one engine of growth

cards.title: Sticky
cards.text: Customers stay. Grow when new customers arrive faster than others leave.

cards.title: Viral
cards.text: Customers bring customers. Grow when each one brings more than one new user.

cards.title: Paid
cards.text: You buy customers. Grow when a customer's lifetime value exceeds what it costs to acquire them.

scenes.banner: Pick one engine, find the metric that drives it, and run experiments to improve that metric.

beats.say: Once you have fit, how do you grow? Ries describes three engines of growth. The sticky engine: customers stay, and you grow when new ones arrive faster than others leave.
The viral engine: customers bring customers. You grow when each user brings in more than one new user.
The paid engine: you buy customers with advertising or sales. You grow when a customer's lifetime value is higher than the cost of acquiring them.
Pick one engine, find the metric that drives it, and keep experimenting to improve that metric. The scientific method doesn't stop at fit.

steps.title: Operators need a diagnostic platform
steps.text: Turbines stop 5–40% of the time; their data is lost.

steps.title: Traffic-light grid, then a dashboard
steps.text: Each prototype answered one question from operators.

steps.title: They want the diagnosis, not the platform
steps.text: Value lay in the analysis, not in the software.

steps.title: Pivot to SmartCast services
steps.text: Same data, sold as a service per turbine per month.

beats.say: Let's see the whole method in a real case. SMARTIVE's hypothesis: wind-farm operators need a platform to diagnose their turbines, which stop between five and forty percent of the time while their data is lost.
The experiments: first a simple traffic-light grid of turbines, then a web dashboard with alarms. Each prototype answered one question from operators.
The evidence: operators did not want another platform to run. What they valued was the diagnosis itself.
The decision: pivot to SmartCast services, the same data and algorithms, sold as a service per turbine per month. A new value proposition, a new revenue model, and a new go-to-market.

scenes.label: Takeaway
scenes.sub: Lean Startup is the scientific method applied to business: use it to search for product–market fit, and treat your go-to-market as hypotheses to test before you scale.

beats.say: To sum up. Lean Startup is the scientific method applied to business: observe, write falsifiable hypotheses, run the smallest experiment, measure what matters, and decide.
Use it to search for product–market fit. And once you are close, keep using it for your go-to-market: segment, message, channel and price are hypotheses too. Test them before you scale.
